cards.title: Increase First-Order AOV to Fund Higher CPA
cards.summary: Shift revenue earlier in the customer relationship by raising first-purchase AOV or defaulting to subscription, so you can afford to spend harder on acquisition without inflating CAC proportionally.
cards.use_when: Repricing offers, designing bundles, or deciding whether to push paid acquisition harder on product selection, PDP or bundle strategy.
steps: Recognize that acquisition cost is easier to justify when the first transaction collects more cash. IM8's move to quarterly ordering appears (early evidence) to have worked for them by pulling more revenue forward.
Ask whether you can raise first-purchase AOV without letting CAC inflate at the same rate — otherwise the extra revenue buys nothing.
Choose a mechanism: create new bundles, push existing bundles harder in ads and on the PDP, or default customers into a subscription option at checkout.
The goal is to collect more cash up front, which then lets you push cost-per-acquisition harder than a lower-AOV competitor could.

Model the trade-off explicitly: higher first-order value buys a wider acceptable payback window, but only if the increased price does not suppress conversion to the point that CAC climbs alongside it.
caveats: IM8's quarterly-subscription shift showed early results only; treat it as a test, not a proven universal tactic.
Source author notes 99.9% of operators cannot safely push CPA payback to seven or eight months like IM8 — that requires enormous capital and is described as ridiculously risky.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Clone a Winning Ad Script Across Personas
cards.summary: Find one winning ad script structure, then multiply creative volume by rerunning the same skeleton against many different personas and audiences.
cards.use_when: Scaling acquisition creative volume after identifying at least one ad that reliably converts on your store.
steps: Identify the single winning ad or ad structure — in IM8's case, a 'timeline' or 'clock' mechanism-based script.
Keep the same script skeleton, creative type and overall structure rather than reinventing the format.
Re-run that identical skeleton against different personas and audience segments (IM8 ran it on joints, metapause, alpha, GP1, gut audiences).
This multiplies creative volume many times over without needing a brand-new winning concept each time.
Pair each persona variation with a matching landing page (see the persona-routing card) so the offer stays consistent from ad to page.
caveats: Depends on first having a genuine winner; cloning a non-winning script just scales waste.
Persona variations must stay truthful to the product — do not invent benefits per persona.

cards.title: Route Persona Ads to Matching Landing Pages
cards.summary: If you change the persona in the ad, make sure the landing page speaks to that same persona — mismatched messaging wastes the targeting.
cards.use_when: Building or updating landing pages and PDPs to match acquisition creative targeting different customer segments.
steps: Decide which persona each ad targets before building the creative.
Build or adapt a dedicated landing page for that persona rather than sending all traffic to one generic page.
Ensure the headline, copy, mechanism and imagery on the landing page match the ad's framing.
IM8's approach: change the persona in the ad, then route that traffic to a persona-specific page so the message stays consistent from click to page.
Audit existing campaigns for persona-to-page mismatches and fix the highest-spend ones first.
caveats: More landing pages means more maintenance and testing overhead; several similar personas may share a page if the message holds.
The source frames this as a general conversion principle, not a tested numeric uplift claim.

cards.title: Sell the Mechanism, Not the Benefit
cards.summary: Lead copy and scripts with the unique mechanism behind the result rather than restating the end benefit everyone claims.
cards.use_when: Writing ad scripts, PDP copy or landing pages where differentiation from competing products is weak.
steps: Identify the specific mechanism, ingredient, delivery format or process that makes your product produce the benefit.
Build the ad script and page copy around explaining that mechanism rather than repeating the benefit.
IM8 does this well — the source calls it a core fundamental of copywriting and script writing they execute on.
Use the mechanism as the recurring spine of the script skeleton you then multiply across personas.
Keep benefit as the payoff, but make mechanism the differentiated argument.
caveats: This is presented as a copywriting fundamental, not a measured benchmark; mechanism claims must be truthful and supportable.

cards.title: Equity Ambassador Deals Instead of Per-Post Fees
cards.summary: Pay long-term partners in equity rather than per-post fees so the cost becomes a smaller percentage of revenue as growth compounds.
cards.use_when: Structuring long-term brand ambassador or influencer partnerships where the relationship will be ongoing and revenue is expected to grow.
steps: Track ambassador and royalty costs as a named line item in your P&L so the percentage of revenue is visible.
IM8 saw that percentage fall from 14% (Q2) to 6.2% (July) as revenue grew, because contracted equity partners become proportionally cheaper over time.
Consider equity deals over fee-for-post deals so the cost stays fixed while revenue compounds.
Ability to do this well depends on being a competent operator who understands what the equity deal should actually look like — the structure and terms matter.
Combine with ongoing activations: IM8 ran activations across roughly 12 cities plus trial sample pushes and earned PR to build brand.
caveats: Source author calls this the least transferable part of IM8's playbook — you cannot simply recruit a Beckham-level co-founder.
Does not recommend rushing into equity deals; requires operator sophistication.
The model only gets cheaper if growth actually compounds — it is not a saving if revenue stalls.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Do Not Copy IM8's Aggressive Payback Window
cards.summary: IM8's long CAC payback and negative contribution to fund acquisition are enabled by roughly a billion dollars in funding and are not transferable to normal brands.
cards.use_when: Deciding how long an acceptable customer-acquisition payback window can be for your store's cash position.
steps: Understand IM8 pushed CAC payback periods out to seven to eight months, which the source describes as ridiculously risky and requiring enormous capital.
Recognize they also nearly lost $20M in a quarter on a roughly 400% negative EBITDA margin to crank acquisition — explicitly called not sustainable for most people.
Set your own payback window based on available cash and realistic contribution margin, not IM8's funded position.
If you lack comparable capital, harvest margin earlier and keep payback shorter.
When reviewing any heavily-funded competitor's model, separate what their funding enables from what your unit economics can actually support.
caveats: These IM8 figures are from a specific funded company and are illustrative, not achievable benchmarks for typical operators.
The author frames IM8 acquisition profitability as 'looking pretty sketchy' as payback windows extend.
cards.source_name: I Scraped 700 IM8 Ads And Read Their P&L. Here's The Whole Playbook.docx

cards.title: Watch Cohort Maturity Before Judging Acquisition Profitability
cards.summary: Newer cohorts are not yet mature, so read acquisition profit and early-cohort metrics with caution and reconcile them later as cohorts season.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether your paid acquisition is actually profitable when the most recent customer cohorts are still too young to have full lifetime data.
steps: Recognize that if cohorts haven't matured, current acquisition profitability figures can look either better or worse than the eventual reality.
IM8's contribution (GP) at month six over time was continuing to decline — a signal the author watches closely.
Track the month-six gross profit per customer over successive cohort generations to see the direction of the trend.
Back-of-envelope the metric yourself when official numbers aren't disclosed; do not wait for a shareholder letter to know your own trend.
When a competitor's payback window is being pushed out, treat their stated acquisition profitability as provisional.
caveats: The month-six metric is IM8's chosen measure; pick a lookback window that fits your own repurchase cadence.
Immature cohorts cannot give a final verdict on profitability.
